title: The Awful Crimes of Georgia Tann
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Georgia Tann, a Memphis-based social worker and director of the Tennessee Children's Home Society who kidnapped, falsified records for, and sold thousands of children (roughly 1924-1950) to wealthy adoptive families, mainly in New York and California. They cover her background in Mississippi, her tactics (fake Christmas adoption ads, nurses stealing babies, forged consent papers), the political protection from Judge Camille Kelly, Boss Crump and attorney Abe Waldauer, the sealed-records laws she lobbied for, the deaths of hundreds of children in her care, her death in 1950 before prosecution, the estate lawsuit, and later reunions and cultural references. The episode opens with tour promotion and closes with a listener mail segment about Peanuts.
topics: history of adoption in the United States

segments.title: Show open
segments.summary: Standard show opening and production credit.

segments.title: Trigger warning and introduction to Georgia Tann
segments.summary: Hosts give a trigger warning about crimes against children and introduce Georgia Tann as a social worker who got rich kidnapping babies and selling them to wealthy families.

segments.title: Orphans and the history of adoption
segments.summary: Discussion of the vulnerability of orphans in the 19th century, the orphan train system, and how modern adoption as a concept in the US is less than a century old.
topics: history of adoption in the United States

segments.title: Unwed mothers and Tann's early life
segments.summary: Hosts describe the stigma faced by unwed mothers and the homes that hid pregnancies, then cover Georgia Tann's Mississippi upbringing, her judge father, and her age-15 idea to profit from placing children with wealthy couples.

segments.title: Early career and the Rose Harvey case
segments.summary: Tann studies law, becomes a social worker in Mississippi, and steals a two-year-old boy from Rose Harvey after a false unfit-mother document. Her relationship with a female partner and her firing are discussed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break in the episode.

segments.title: Tennessee Children's Home Society and famous clients
segments.summary: Tann moves to Tennessee Children's Home Society, selling more than 5,000 children from 1924 to 1950, earning around a million dollars. Notable adoptive clients include Joan Crawford, Lana Turner, Dick Powell, June Allyson, Pearl Buck, and Rick Flair.

segments.title: Lack of records and tactics overview
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the lack of paper trails for stolen children and Tann's contempt for poor mothers, plus her marketing tactics.

segments.title: Orphanage deaths and adoption as a business
segments.summary: Tann runs a Memphis orphanage where babies die; hosts describe the adoption as a business that marketed babies as blank slates and falsified parent origins.

segments.title: Christmas baby drives and adoption fees
segments.summary: Tann ran Christmas adoption ads in the Memphis Press-Scimitar, and charged out-of-state wealthy clients around five thousand dollars instead of state-set fees of about seven hundred dollars.
topics: wealthy clients New York and California

segments.title: Targeting wealthy adopters and kidnapping methods
segments.summary: Hosts explain that Tann targeted wealthy parents who believed they were adopting from good families, and describe kidnapping from neighborhoods using a limousine.

segments.title: Hospital theft and forged papers
segments.summary: Tann told new mothers their infants had died, and used forged adoption papers signed by anesthetized mothers, plus a network of nurses and impostors.

segments.title: Judge Camille Kelly's complicity
segments.summary: Judge Camille Kelly supplied roughly 20 percent of the children Tann obtained, bent rules and falsified records; the hosts also discuss Barbara Raymond's book estimate and a Catholic orphanage hiding children.

segments.title: Deaths of children and mass grave
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the 500 to 600 children estimated to have died at Tann's orphanage, most unreported, Memphis's highest infant mortality rate in 1932, and a 2016 memorial over a mass grave. Sexual abuse of adopted children is mentioned.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Second break in the episode.

segments.title: Boss Crump and the political protection
segments.summary: Mayor Ed Crump, known as Boss Crump, and attorney Abe Waldauer protected Tann; Tann used Judge Kelly to get laws changed through the legislature.

segments.title: Tennessee adoption laws and sealed records
segments.summary: The 1852 Tennessee adoption law and its requirements are contrasted with Tann's practices; a notary replaced judge certification, and Tann lobbied for sealed adoption records that hid children from birth families.

segments.title: Sealed records persist
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the continued sealing of pre-1980s adoption records, including those of Tann's victims, and how falsified records hinder reunions.

segments.title: Investigation, death, and the newspaper exposé
segments.summary: Governor Gordon Browning ordered an investigation led by Robert Taylor, but held it back until Tann died of uterine cancer on September 15, 1950 at age 58. Reporters in Memphis broke the story just before her death.

segments.title: Estate lawsuit and Anne Atwood
segments.summary: The state sued Tann's estate over excess adoption fees, recovering about fifty thousand dollars of the five hundred thousand sought. Tann had adopted her partner Anne Atwood shortly before death.

segments.title: Reunions and Denny Glad's advocacy
segments.summary: Almas Sipple recognized Tann on Unsolved Mysteries in 1990 and reunited with her daughter Sandra; Denny Glad and Tennessee's Right to Know push to open records.

segments.title: Pop culture references and further reading
segments.summary: Hosts mention the 1993 TV movie Stolen Babies with Mary Tyler Moore, a band with the same name, Octavia Spencer's interest in the story, and Barbara Bisantz Raymond's book Baby Thief.

segments.title: Listener mail: Peanuts correction
segments.summary: A listener corrects an earlier episode, noting that Frieda, not Sally, talked about her naturally curly hair in the Peanuts episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing reminders to contact the show and production credits.
